instruction: Independently review every assigned ID in full scenario context; examine the first finding and any changed question. A pass on changed content also rechecks the repair. Do not edit the bank.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which two responses could follow D1's reaction to your re-offer?

options.text: Use the new lane if F1 can reach it
Notice space D1 leaves for F2 if D1 follows
Pass to yourself through D1

originalQuestion.explanation: D1's response creates the next decision: use the lane, or exploit the space that the defender left.

originalQuestion.prompt: Move YOU to a support point above the shaded return line.
originalQuestion.explanation: The point gives F2 a new relationship to read while keeping D1 visible.

manifest.riskReason: Goalie coverage changes the rebound state; the static frame cannot certify a shot or recovery outcome.

originalQuestion.prompt: The goalie covers before you arrive. What do you re-read?
originalQuestion.explanation: The loose-puck option is gone, so identify who has the puck and where F1 can support before choosing the next pressure or reset.

originalQuestion.prompt: What should YOU communicate on the backcheck?

options.text: D1 has F1; I am tracking F2 toward the left net
I am chasing the puck only
F2 does not receive

originalQuestion.explanation: The call identifies the uncovered runner and the teammate pressure.

originalQuestion.prompt: Move YOU between F2 and the left net.
originalQuestion.explanation: This point improves the defended net-side relationship to F2 and keeps F1 visible.

manifest.riskReason: Blue-line practice reset and offside distinction are rule/timing dependent.

originalQuestion.prompt: What should YOU communicate during the reset?

options.text: Reset is the drill instruction; I will check F1 before restarting
The still frame proves offside
The pass must happen now

originalQuestion.explanation: The call keeps the practice instruction separate from a formal ruling and adds a restart check.

manifest.riskReason: Blue-line restart readiness depends on a stated practice condition and timing.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which two cues can delay the restart?

options.text: The coach has not restarted the rep
F1's route or support has changed
The blue line is painted

originalQuestion.explanation: The stated restart and current player relationships determine readiness; paint alone does not.

manifest.riskReason: The blue-line reset position is rule/timing dependent.

originalQuestion.prompt: Move YOU behind the right blue line with F1 visible.
originalQuestion.explanation: This point completes the practice reset while retaining the carrier in view.

manifest.riskReason: A formal offside decision requires rule and timing context absent from the freeze.

originalQuestion.prompt: What cue tells you this practice reset is ready to resume?
originalQuestion.explanation: Wait for the coach's restart and re-check F1's route. The position alone does not establish a formal rule call or timing.

originalQuestion.prompt: D1 drops toward F2 before your touch. What should change first?

options.text: Protect the puck and scan a different exit
Pass inside immediately because F2 was the first outlet
Stop reading and skate into D1

originalQuestion.explanation: D1 closing the middle changes the named outlet; protecting the puck buys a chance to find a wall-side or return option.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which two checks make a re-offer useful?

options.text: Whether D1 follows the new angle
Whether F1 can still see and reach YOU
Whether the same route is still blocked after you move

originalQuestion.explanation: D1's response and F1's sightline explain availability; matching the old route can keep the line blocked.

originalQuestion.prompt: F2 carries toward the middle instead of returning. What should YOU do?

options.text: Adjust support relative to F2 and call the available lane
Stay on the old return line and stop scanning
Skate directly into F2's path

originalQuestion.explanation: F2's carry changes the carrier-support relationship. Move with space and communication while keeping D1 visible.

originalQuestion.prompt: Move YOU to an approach point below the rebound that keeps the net and D1 visible.
originalQuestion.explanation: This point changes YOU toward the rebound while keeping the net-side defender in view.

originalQuestion.prompt: D1 reaches the puck first. What should you update?

options.text: Whether to support F1 or pressure the new carrier
Assume your second shot is still available
Skate through D1 to the net

originalQuestion.explanation: D1 winning the loose puck changes possession and your job. Read F1 and the new carrier before choosing pressure or support.

manifest.riskReason: A goalie/rebound state and any second shot depend on future possession and execution.

originalQuestion.prompt: What would you need to see before suggesting a second shot?
originalQuestion.explanation: Identify who controls the rebound, D1's coverage, and whether a lane to the net or F1 remains. The freeze does not prove a second shot is available.

originalQuestion.prompt: D1 follows outside and F2 opens inside. What becomes worth checking?

options.text: Whether F2 can now receive from your protected position
Whether to keep carrying without looking
Whether D1 has become a teammate

originalQuestion.explanation: D1's movement changes the inside lane. Check F2's reachability before releasing or carrying again.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which player is behind YOU in this neutral-zone picture?

options.text: F2
D1
YOU

originalQuestion.explanation: D1 is behind and inside YOU relative to the +x attack.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which two cues should change a carry decision?

options.text: Whether the forward lane stays open
Whether D1 can close from inside
That F2 is wide so the carry must continue

originalQuestion.explanation: The lane and defender movement explain whether carrying preserves space; F2 is an option, not a command.

originalQuestion.prompt: Arrange the open-space scan.

options.text: Check the lane and D1
Take the controlled touch
Re-read F2 and the next lane

originalQuestion.explanation: A small touch earns new information; the next decision comes from the changed relationships.

originalQuestion.prompt: Move YOU into an example forward lane that leaves room from F2.
originalQuestion.explanation: The point moves +x into the open lane while leaving F2 on a separate wide route.

originalQuestion.prompt: D1 turns and reaches the wide lane before your next touch. What should you change?

options.text: Protect or use F2 if that lane remains reachable
Continue wide because the first lane was open
Stop and wait for D1 to choose

originalQuestion.explanation: D1 has changed the lane. Check whether protection or F2 now gives a safer continuation.

originalQuestion.prompt: What movement from D1 would make you stop carrying forward?
originalQuestion.explanation: A turn that closes the lane ahead or cuts off your support should trigger a re-read. Explain where F2 or a protected touch could replace the carry.

originalQuestion.prompt: What does an inside approach try to preserve?

options.text: The middle and the route to the net
A chance to chase F2 wide immediately
A predictable carrier path regardless of movement

originalQuestion.explanation: Inside positioning protects the middle while showing the carrier a wall-side route; F2 still needs a scan.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which attacker has moved beyond YOU toward the left net?

options.text: F1
F2
The goalie

originalQuestion.explanation: The briefing identifies F1 as ahead of YOU toward the left net.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which two details guide a useful recovery?

options.text: F1's route to the net
F2's separate wide position
A second reach from behind even if the picture changes

originalQuestion.explanation: The carrier route and second attacker shape recovery. A repeated reach may leave the net-side relationship worse.

originalQuestion.prompt: Arrange the recovery response.

options.text: Recognize the missed reach
Recover toward the net-side space
Re-check F1 and F2

originalQuestion.explanation: The response prioritizes a useful relationship and then updates both attackers.

originalQuestion.prompt: Move YOU to a recovery point between the attackers and the left net.
originalQuestion.explanation: This point moves toward the defended net-side lane and keeps F2 visible across the ice.

originalQuestion.prompt: F1 slows toward the boards while F2 drives middle. What should update?

options.text: Your recovery should protect the new middle threat while staying connected to F1
Keep chasing F1 into the boards
Ignore F2 because the first reach was on F1

originalQuestion.explanation: F1 and F2 changed jobs in the picture. Protect the middle and keep a playable relationship to F1.

originalQuestion.prompt: Why can recovering toward the net be better than reaching again from behind?
originalQuestion.explanation: The net-side relationship limits the dangerous lane and keeps both attackers in view. A second reach may miss and leave the middle unprotected.

originalQuestion.prompt: What belongs in your backcheck read?

options.text: F2's route toward the right net
D1's ability to stay with F1
The puck alone, without scanning F2

originalQuestion.explanation: The uncovered runner and teammate pressure define the backcheck job; puck chasing alone can abandon F2.

originalQuestion.prompt: D1 moves into your shooting line and F2 becomes clearly reachable. What deserves a new look?

options.text: A cross-ice pass to F2
A shot through D1 without checking
A pass behind the net to no one

originalQuestion.explanation: D1 changed the shooting lane while F2 became more reachable, so the pass deserves a fresh read.

originalQuestion.prompt: Why does YOU have a different first job from F2?

options.text: F2 is closer to the loose puck
YOU owns the puck
D1 is a navy player

originalQuestion.explanation: F2 is the nearer navy player to the loose puck; YOU can support from above.

manifest.riskReason: Blue-line side language is rule/geometry dependent.

originalQuestion.prompt: Where is YOU relative to the right blue line in this practice?

options.text: Behind it toward the right net
Inside it toward centre ice
At the left goal line

originalQuestion.explanation: YOU is inside the right blue line area in the +x attack picture; the reset asks for a move behind it.

manifest.riskReason: Reset readiness depends on a stated practice condition and timing.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which two facts determine whether the reset is ready?

options.text: The coach's stated reset instruction
Where F1 and F2 are when the rep restarts
A silent offside verdict from the still image

originalQuestion.explanation: The practice instruction and player locations are visible cues. A formal call needs more timing information than this freeze.

manifest.riskReason: The reset sequence is tied to a blue-line practice condition.

originalQuestion.prompt: Arrange the stated reset steps.

options.text: Hear the reset instruction
Move behind the blue line under control
Re-check F1 before starting again

originalQuestion.explanation: The sequence follows the coach instruction and checks the carrier before the next action.

manifest.riskReason: The blue-line reset destination is rule/geometry dependent.

originalQuestion.prompt: Move YOU to an example reset point behind the right blue line.
originalQuestion.explanation: This point shifts YOU farther toward the right-net side while keeping F1 and D1 visible.

manifest.riskReason: Restart timing and formal-rule context are explicitly in play.

originalQuestion.prompt: F1 keeps waiting after YOU resets. What is the useful next check?

options.text: Whether F1 still has a reachable route and whether the coach has restarted the rep
Assume the pass must happen now
Make a full rule call from the picture

originalQuestion.explanation: The waiting changes the practice timing cue. Re-check F1 and the stated restart rather than inventing a formal ruling.

manifest.riskReason: A formal offside decision requires timing and rule context absent from the freeze.

originalQuestion.prompt: What information is still missing before a formal offside decision?
originalQuestion.explanation: The coach's reset is visible, but timing and rule context are not. Follow the drill instruction and avoid treating the freeze as a formal ruling.

findings.issue: The position prompt relies on a “shaded return line” that is not a rink marking or separately rendered object.
findings.evidence: exp26-u11-004-q9 asks to move above “the shaded return line”; its setup only supplies YOU (10,4), F2 (14,-3), and D1 (12,0.5), with no rendered line.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact question patch: replace prompt with "Move YOU to a support point above the direct return lane between your old position and F2." Replace explanation with "This point gives F2 a new support relationship while keeping D1 visible; the lane is inferred from the named players, not an unrendered shade."

findings.issue: Both the communication key and position target send the gold defender toward the wrong net.
findings.evidence: The briefing says Navy attacks +x/right and YOU is gold returning toward the right net; q7 keys “tracking F2 toward the left net” and q9 asks “between F2 and the left net” (F2 is navy at x17, YOU x12).
findings.recommendedChange: Exact patches: q7 option a text -> "D1 has F1; I am tracking F2 toward the right net". q9 prompt -> "Move YOU between F2 and the right net." q9 explanation -> "This point improves the defended net-side relationship to F2 and keeps F1 visible; the recovery route remains conditional on F2’s movement."

findings.issue: The reset destination moves YOU farther toward +x even though the briefing requires returning to the neutral-zone side of the right blue line.
findings.evidence: The setup has YOU at (10,-3) and says YOU is beyond the right blue line; q9 reference is (12.4,-3.4), which moves farther right. The supplied catalog version uses an illustrative neutral-side point at (6,-3).
findings.recommendedChange: Exact patch: keep the prompt, replace reference with {"x":6,"y":-3}, and replace explanation with "This point places YOU on the neutral-zone side of the right blue line for this practice reset while keeping F1 visible; it is illustrative, not a formal offside verdict."

findings.issue: The multi-select key excludes a third live check that the prompt reasonably allows.
findings.evidence: q2 asks which two checks make a re-offer useful, but option c, “Whether the same route is still blocked after you move,” is also a valid check; the explanation itself says matching the old route can keep the line blocked.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact question patch: change prompt to "Which two positive signs make a re-offer useful?" and replace option c with {"id":"c","text":"Whether D1 has become a teammate"}; retain answer ["a","b"].

findings.issue: The position key describes the destination as below the rebound, but the reference is above the puck on the y axis.
findings.evidence: The puck is at (23,-5), while q4 reference is (22.1,-4.1); with the source coordinate convention, -4.1 is above -5. The prompt says “below the rebound.”
findings.recommendedChange: Exact patch: replace prompt with "Move YOU to an approach point just above the rebound that keeps the net and D1 visible." Replace explanation with "This point approaches the loose puck from above while keeping the net-side defender in view."

findings.issue: The scene key calls D1 behind YOU, but D1 is farther up ice on the +x attack.
findings.evidence: Navy attacks +x; YOU is at (-8,-4) and D1 is at (-2,2). q1 keys “D1” for “Which player is behind YOU,” although x=-2 is ahead of x=-8.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact question patch: replace prompt with "Which player is ahead of YOU in this neutral-zone picture?"; retain answer ["b"] and replace explanation with "D1 is ahead of YOU on the +x direction and sits inside the route."

findings.issue: The multi-select key marks an incorrect defensive aim as correct.
findings.evidence: q2 asks what an inside approach tries to preserve. Option b says “A chance to chase F2 wide immediately,” but the explanation says F2 still needs a scan; the correct preservation is the middle/net route in option a.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact patch: change answer from ["a","b"] to ["a"]. Replace explanation with "Inside positioning protects the middle and route to the net while showing the carrier a wall-side route; F2 remains a separate scan, not an immediate chase."

findings.issue: The key contradicts the attack direction and coordinates.
findings.evidence: Gold attacks -x; YOU is at (13,2) and F1 at (15,4). F1 is to the +x side of YOU, so it has not moved beyond YOU toward the left net as the prompt states.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact question patch: replace prompt with "Which attacker is closer to YOU after the missed reach?"; retain answer ["a"] and replace explanation with "F1 is the nearer attacker to YOU in this freeze; the picture does not by itself establish a movement path toward the left net."

findings.issue: The coaching key sends the gold attack toward the wrong net.
findings.evidence: The briefing says Gold attacks -x/left. q2 option a says “F2’s route toward the right net,” while q4 and the rest of the scene defend the left-net route.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact patch: replace option a text with "F2’s route toward the left net"; retain answer ["a","b"] and replace explanation with "The uncovered runner toward the left net and D1’s pressure on F1 define the backcheck job."

findings.issue: The nearest-player key contradicts the supplied coordinates, even though the coach separately assigns F2 as retriever.
findings.evidence: Puck is at (23,-9); YOU at (21,-5) is about 4.5 m away, while F2 at (19,-9) is 4 m away. q1 says F2 is closer without reconciling the explicit retriever assignment.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact question patch: replace option a text with "The coach assigned F2 as the retriever" and replace explanation with "F2 has a different first job because the coach assigned that retrieval; YOU supports from above even though the frozen distances are close." Retain answer ["a"].

findings.issue: One distractor in each affected question is cartoonishly impossible or unsafe instead of a credible U11 misconception, reducing the quality of the decision contrast.
findings.evidence: The affected distractors are: exp26-u11-003-q8 “Pass to yourself through D1”; exp26b-u11-001-q5 “Stop reading and skate into D1”; exp26b-u11-004-q5 “Skate directly into F2’s path”; exp26b-u11-006-q5 “Skate through D1 to the net”; exp26b-u11-007-q5 “Whether D1 has become a teammate”; exp26b-u11-021-q5 “A pass behind the net to no one.”
findings.recommendedChange: Exact option patches: exp26-u11-003-q8 option c -> "Keep offering the same lane without changing your angle"; exp26b-u11-001-q5 option c -> "Carry into the middle without checking whether D1 has closed it"; exp26b-u11-004-q5 option c -> "Stay on the old return line without checking F2’s route"; exp26b-u11-006-q5 option c -> "Keep chasing the rebound as if D1 had not reached it"; exp26b-u11-007-q5 option c -> "Keep the same carry without rechecking F2"; exp26b-u11-021-q5 option c -> "Hold the puck without checking whether F2 becomes reachable".

scenarios.title: Step out of the shaded lane
scenarios.objective: Recognize that a teammate can be nearby yet unavailable on a direct passing line.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. F1 has possession. YOU are a nearby receiver, but D1 stands between you and the puck. F2 is farther across the ice. The task is to improve your own availability.
cues: D1 occupies the direct F1-to-YOU line.
F2 offers a separate angle.
Being nearest is different from having a clear lane.

sources.title: 7 Principles for Coaches: Vision & Scanning
sources.section: Key Information to Identify; Reading Pressure / Corner Situations
sources.use: Supports checking teammates and pressure; answers are original scene analysis.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. Static line obstruction is visible; interception timing and a uniquely best pass are not proven. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Which player stands on the direct line between F1 and YOU?

options.text: F2
D1
No player

questions.explanation: D1 sits between the carrier and your current receiving spot.

questions.prompt: What could make your support more useful?

options.text: Create a different angle from F1
Keep track of D1 as you move
Stand closer even if D1 stays in the same line

questions.explanation: Changing the angle can expose a lane. Closing distance alone does not remove the obstruction.

questions.prompt: Arrange a simple re-offer routine.

options.text: Notice the blocked line
Move into a different passing angle
Check whether F1 can still see and reach you

questions.explanation: This is a suggested way to solve this obstruction; the carrier may choose another action meanwhile.

questions.prompt: Move YOU away from D1’s current passing shadow.
questions.explanation: The sample shifts across the line instead of only closer to F1. Other separated angles may work.

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 follows your new route. What is a useful next read?

options.text: Assume the lane must still be open
Stay in the new spot without checking F1
Look for another angle or space opened for F2

questions.explanation: A defender’s response changes which lane is useful. Your movement can also help a teammate.

questions.prompt: How would you tell the difference between “closer” and “more available” here?
questions.explanation: Describe the carrier-to-receiver line and the defender in it, rather than relying only on distance.

questions.prompt: What is the useful communication after D1 blocks the first line?

options.text: I will re-offer above the line; check whether you can reach me
The first lane is open even if the picture changes
F2 must stay wide and never move

questions.explanation: The message names the changed angle and keeps F1's pass conditional on reachability.

questions.prompt: Which two responses could follow D1's reaction to your re-offer?

options.text: Use the new lane if F1 can reach it
Notice space D1 leaves for F2 if D1 follows
Hold the same direct lane while D1 remains between F1 and YOU

questions.explanation: D1's response creates the next decision: use the lane, or exploit the space that the defender left.

questions.prompt: Move YOU across the blocked line into a visible support angle.
questions.explanation: This point changes the F1-to-YOU line and keeps F2 separate.

questions.prompt: F1 carries while D1 follows you. Explain the value of your movement.
questions.explanation: Your movement can pull D1 and open F2 or F1's carry lane. Call the open space, then re-check it because D1 may recover.

scenarios.title: A new job after your pass
scenarios.objective: Plan off-puck movement after a completed pass without assuming an immediate return.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU have just passed to F2, who now owns the puck. D1 lies between your old position and F2. This freeze begins after reception, not during flight.
cues: F2 owns the puck now.
YOU no longer need to carry it.
D1 shades the old return line.

sources.title: Hockey Canada U11 Player Pathway
sources.section: U11 Skills Matrix, printed page 22 (PDF page 22)
sources.use: Age-topic support only; no approval of these answers.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. Pass-and-follow is an age-topic connection. The support route is original and has no timing validation. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: What changed when the stated pass finished?

options.text: YOU kept possession through the completed pass
F2 became the puck carrier
Both YOU and F2 now own the puck

questions.explanation: The briefing and ownership both identify F2 as the receiver in possession.

questions.prompt: Which choices keep YOU involved without owning the puck?

options.text: Offer a fresh return angle
Notice where D1 follows
Remain in the old return line without checking D1

questions.explanation: Off-puck support means remaining useful as the carrier and defence change.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested continuation after reception.

options.text: Recognize that F2 now has possession
Find space outside the old return line
Show a new option and read D1 again

questions.explanation: The routine begins from actual reception. It does not promise a second pass.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to offer a new return angle for F2.
questions.explanation: The example moves beyond the old obstruction. A shorter lateral option can also work if it creates a usable line.

questions.prompt: If F2 carries forward instead of returning the puck, what could YOU do?

options.text: Adjust support to F2’s new location
Insist that F2 pass back immediately
Stay at the original pass location without another look

questions.explanation: Support follows the actual carrier. The initial pass does not require a scripted return.

questions.prompt: What might your movement accomplish even if F2 never passes back?
questions.explanation: It could offer support, move a defender or leave another lane available. Identify which relationship you expect to change.

questions.prompt: After F2 receives, what should YOU communicate?

options.text: I am changing the support angle; tell me if the return lane opens
The puck must come straight back
My first pass is complete because I passed

questions.explanation: The message matches the new carrier and keeps the return conditional while support continues.

questions.prompt: Which two details decide where to support F2?

options.text: F2's direction with the puck
D1's coverage of the old return line
The fact that YOU passed once

questions.explanation: The current carrier and defender coverage describe the new job; the earlier pass does not fix the next spot.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a support point above the direct return lane between your old position and F2.
questions.explanation: This point gives F2 a new support relationship while keeping D1 visible; the lane is inferred from the named players.

questions.prompt: F2 carries toward the middle and D1 turns with F2. What do you do next?
questions.explanation: Match support to F2's new position, keep a usable lane, and communicate the space F1 or YOU can offer if D1 follows.

scenarios.title: Find the loose rebound first
scenarios.objective: Separate a loose puck from a promised rebound goal.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. The coach states that F1’s previous shot came loose to the goalie’s side. YOU are arriving away from the puck. No goal or next touch is assumed.
cues: The loose puck is on the positive-y side of the goal area.
D1 stands closer to the middle.
YOU must locate the puck before planning a second action.

sources.title: USA Hockey: Skill Progressions for Youth Hockey
sources.use: Lists skill/team topics; Canadian adaptation and answers remain experimental.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. Rebound shooting is a topic connection; neither save physics nor arrival order is simulated. No net-front contact is instructed. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Where is the puck relative to the goalie at this freeze?

options.text: At centre ice
Off to one side of the goalie, still loose
Already in the goalie’s glove

questions.explanation: The puck is beside the goalie’s current area and has no owner. It is neither at centre ice nor held by the goalie.

questions.prompt: Which cues matter for your next approach?

options.text: Where the loose puck actually is
Where D1 is relative to the approach
The assumption that the next touch must be a shot

questions.explanation: Locate both puck and obstruction. A second chance still needs a real recovery and shooting opportunity.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested rebound-read routine.

options.text: Locate the loose puck
Check the approach and establish control if possible
Reassess a shot or pass

questions.explanation: This example emphasizes control and a new read. An immediate touch could be appropriate if the actual arrival supports it.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to show an approach toward the loose-puck side.
questions.explanation: The example approaches from outside D1’s current middle position. It is not proof that YOU arrive first.

questions.prompt: If the goalie covers the puck before YOU arrive, what changes?

options.text: The puck is still available for a rebound shot
YOU can assume a goal
The previous loose-puck plan no longer applies

questions.explanation: A covered puck is a different state. Do not continue acting on the earlier loose-puck assumption.

questions.prompt: What extra information would you need before predicting a second shot?
questions.explanation: You might need puck movement, defender speed, control and whether play is still active. A static loose puck does not establish them.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call while approaching the rebound?

options.text: Puck below the circle; D1 is between it and the net
The second shot is ours
F1 must shoot next

questions.explanation: The call names the actual puck and defender, which helps F1 understand the recovery read.

questions.prompt: Which two changes would alter the rebound plan?

options.text: D1 controls the puck
F1 becomes a reachable support option
The net stays at the same end

questions.explanation: Possession and support change the next job; the net location alone does not decide the play.

questions.prompt: Move YOU below the puck on its net-side approach.
questions.explanation: This point approaches the loose puck while preserving D1 and the net in view.

questions.prompt: The goalie covers before you arrive. What do you re-read?
questions.explanation: The loose-puck option is gone, so identify who has the puck and where F1 can support before choosing the next pressure or reset.

scenarios.title: Backcheck the uncovered runner
scenarios.objective: Separate the carrier’s pressure from a second attacker’s route.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU are gold, returning toward the right net. The coach has assigned gold D1 to the navy puck carrier F1 for this rep. Navy F2 is moving through the other side of the middle; this movement is stated rather than animated.
cues: D1 has the carrier assignment for this rep.
F2 is a separate navy runner.
YOU defend the right net.

sources.title: USA Hockey: Skill Progressions for Youth Hockey
sources.use: Lists skill/team topics; Canadian adaptation and answers remain experimental.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. The manual names backchecking and defensive positioning. This two-defender assignment is an original drill constraint, not a universal system. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Who is already assigned to the carrier in this practice rep?

options.text: Gold D1
Gold YOU
Navy F2

questions.explanation: The briefing explicitly assigns gold D1 to navy F1, who owns the puck. That assignment creates a separate support decision for YOU.

questions.prompt: Before choosing your backcheck route, what information belongs in the read?

options.text: Whether F2 can receive toward the middle
Whether D1 still has pressure on F1
Whether YOU can see both the runner and puck

questions.explanation: These three cues connect your responsibility to the live play. The initial assignment may need to change if D1 loses the carrier.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested backcheck check-in.

options.text: Identify who is pressuring the carrier.
Find the separate runner and choose an inside recovery route.
Keep checking for a pass or a changed assignment.

questions.explanation: The routine helps avoid two defenders following the puck while another attacker is available. It is not a command to ignore a reachable puck.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward a useful defensive relationship with F2 and the right net. Multiple recovery spots may work.
questions.explanation: The reference places YOU nearer the right net than F2 and close to the runner’s route. This illustrates a goal-side relationship; it does not prove interception timing or prescribe a fixed gap.

questions.prompt: If D1 falls behind F1 and calls for help, how should YOU respond?

options.text: Keep the original assignment without looking again.
Recheck the immediate net threat and communicate who can cover F2.
Automatically skate to the far corner.

questions.explanation: New pressure information can change the responsibilities. Helping on the carrier may be needed, but F2’s route should remain part of the decision rather than disappearing from the read.

questions.prompt: What would make your backcheck different from simply skating toward the puck?

Stay slot-side as if F2 still controls
Chase the old loose-puck spot

questions.prompt: How can YOU help a corner retrieval without being closest?
questions.explanation: A slot-side angle gives F2 a visible outlet and can receive a pass while leaving the corner carrier room. It remains conditional on D1's coverage.

scenarios.title: Reset behind the blue line
scenarios.objective: Use a practice reset location while separating it from a formal rule judgement.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks +x. F1 carries near the right blue line; YOU is just inside the line and F2 is behind the play. D1 is farther inside. The coach calls for a reset behind the line before the next rep.
cues: The coach has stated a practice reset.
YOU is near the right blue line.
The still scene does not make a full offside call.

sources.title: USA Hockey: Skill Progressions for Youth Hockey

questions.prompt: Where is YOU relative to the right blue line in this practice?

Inside it toward centre ice
At the left goal line

questions.prompt: Which two facts determine whether the reset is ready?

options.text: The coach's stated reset instruction
Where F1 and F2 are when the rep restarts
A silent offside verdict from the still image

questions.explanation: The practice instruction and player locations are visible cues. A formal call needs more timing information than this freeze.

questions.prompt: Arrange the stated reset steps.

options.text: Hear the reset instruction
Move behind the blue line under control
Re-check F1 before starting again

questions.explanation: The sequence follows the coach instruction and checks the carrier before the next action.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example reset point behind the right blue line.
questions.explanation: This point shifts YOU farther toward the right-net side while keeping F1 and D1 visible.

questions.prompt: F1 keeps waiting after YOU resets. What is the useful next check?

options.text: Whether F1 still has a reachable route and whether the coach has restarted the rep
Assume the pass must happen now
Make a full rule call from the picture

questions.explanation: The waiting changes the practice timing cue. Re-check F1 and the stated restart rather than inventing a formal ruling.

questions.prompt: What information is still missing before a formal offside decision?
questions.explanation: The coach's reset is visible, but timing and rule context are not. Follow the drill instruction and avoid treating the freeze as a formal ruling.
